newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman banks on gas to shake up oil-led economy.
newsitem.headline: Oman banks on gas to shake up oil-led economy.

text.p: Oman has banked on four new foreign-backed gas projects to gradually wean the Gulf Arab state away from its near total dependency on oil export earnings, Gulf economists and diplomats said on Wednesday.

Liquefied natural gas (LNG), fertiliser, petrochemical, and aluminium schemes are being put in place for start up between 2000 and 2002 to cut oil's economic predominance and diversify the country's industrial base.

Modest oil output of nearly 900,000 barrels per day (bpd) provides 75 percent of annual state revenue of $5.3 billion, the four projects would at full capacity trim this contribution close to 50 percent, economists said.

But with the government determined to create jobs, develop new infrastructure outside Muscat and reverse a $900 million current account deficit into balance by 2000, potential foreign investors are still questioning how projects will be funded.
"The rates of return for foreign investors in the petrochemical plant and the aluminium smelter still have to be looked at closely," said one Gulf energy investor.

British Petroleum's chemicals division this week were chosen by Oman's Commerce and Industry ministry as its foreign partner to build a $900 petrochemical plant at the Omani town of Sohar, 200 km (125 mile) north of the capital Muscat.

Sohar, the centre of an economically depressed agricultural region and home to a third of the country's 1.5 million Omanis, lacks a pipeline large enough that could carry gas from two major fields in central Oman.
The port town has also been chosen as the site for a proposed $2.4 billion aluminium smelter that would run off methane gas not used at the ethane-based petrochemical plant.
"The big question is who will pay for the pipeline and gas separation units...that will dictate the economics of the two projects," a diplomatic source in Muscat said.
Negotiations on a petrochemical plant in Oman have been underway since the late eighties but stalled on the issue of who would pay for infrastructure -- notably pipeline -- costs.
New pipelines typically cost $1 million per kilometre.
BP has said it is now studying the economics and equity participation in the planned 450,000 tonnes year ethylene and polyethylene plant due on stream between 2001 and 2002.

Some analysts questioned the Commerce ministry's decision to build the petrochemical and-or the aluminium plant at Sohar apparently because of domestic employment and social considerations rather than pure project economics.
"If the Ministry of Petroleum had had their say they would have argued that the projects be at Sur with the LNG and urea (fertiliser)," one Gulf-based oil executive said.
The coastal town of Sur, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Muscat, will be source of the main non-oil foreign exchange earner behind oil in the coming decades.
Exports from a $6 billion LNG project -- backed by leading foreign oil majors -- and a $1 billion gas-fired fertiliser plant are on schedule to begin in the year 2000.

Tanker exports of liquefied gas from the LNG plant are expected to increase government revenues by 18 percent at full capacity while sales of nearly 100,000 bpd of light condensate oil from the same project will also boost state coffers.
Oman's proven gas reserves stand at 16.2 trillion cubic feet though "expected" reserves are 39 trillion cubic feet.
